title: Cell Products: Marrow Harvest Dose, CFU Potency and CAR T Cells
summary: Learn how marrow harvests are planned to a nucleated-cell dose and why pull size matters, why the CFU potency assay cannot give a same-day answer, and how CAR T cells and sipuleucel-T are built.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 43 Hit 8 (marrow harvest dose and pull volume), Hit 13 (CAR structure, 2017 anti-CD19 approvals, sipuleucel-T) and Trap 3 (CFU potency is slow; CD34 flow is same-day; ALDH), checked against the NMDP Marrow Alliance white paper (Murakami 2024; read via a page-fetch tool), Tiwari 2023, Yusoff 2025, Gençer 2017, Fujiwara 2020, Ahmad 2020, Graff 2015 and Sutherland 2021. Qualifications: the source gives a 3.0 × 10⁸ TNC/kg recipient goal, not the reviewer’s 2–3 × 10⁸ viable nucleated cells/kg (flag rv-marrow-harvest-dose); pull volumes range from 5 to 20 mL by technique, not a fixed 3–5 mL (rv-marrow-pull-volume); sipuleucel-T is taught as antigen-pulsed autologous antigen-presenting cells (sources describe it both as an APC-enriched preparation and as a dendritic-cell based therapy, so the reviewer’s wording is not flagged); the 2017 approvals are US FDA rulings and axicabtagene ciloleucel was approved for large B-cell lymphoma (rv-cart-2017-us-approval). Pending (not taught): HPCs as ~1% of marrow cells, the ~700 mL harvest for a 70-kg adult, the general 10–14 day CFU turnaround (only a single study’s 14 days is taught), and the 1–2 hour ALDH turnaround.

objectives: State how a marrow harvest goal is expressed and why smaller pulls are used.
Explain why CD34 flow, not the CFU assay, gives the same-day answer on an HPC product.
Describe the domains of a chimeric antigen receptor and contrast CAR T cells with sipuleucel-T.

scenes.title: Three requests, one cell lab
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: a cell-therapy laboratory gets three requests in one day — (1) a marrow harvest for an unrelated recipient, where the surgeon wants to take big pulls to finish faster; (2) a physician who wants a potency result on an apheresis product “by this afternoon”; (3) an engineered T-cell product for a young patient with relapsed B-cell ALL. Question token: “Which dose, which assay, which receptor?”

cues.text: A cell therapy lab gets three requests in one day: a marrow harvest where the surgeon wants big pulls to finish faster; and a physician who wants a potency result on a stem cell product by this afternoon.
The third is an engineered T cell product for a young patient with relapsed B-cell leukemia.
Which dose, which assay, and which receptor?

props.label: Which dose, which assay, which receptor?

scenes.title: Marrow is harvested to a cell dose
scenes.altText: Schematic harvest card (NMDP Marrow Alliance white paper, Murakami 2024): the NMDP set a goal total nucleated cell (TNC) dose of 3.0 × 10⁸/kg recipient weight as a quality metric; volume-based collections are usually 10–15 mL/kg recipient weight, and the NMDP and many centres cap the volume at 20 mL/kg donor weight; during harvest the goal volume is refined by dividing the requested TNC by the marrow WBC count. Pull card: some centres limit pulls to 5 mL, others take up to 20 mL with stylet replacement; data show higher TNC concentrations with smaller pulls, but the effect on final yield and outcomes is not yet determined.

cues.text: Marrow is collected to a cell dose, not just a volume. The NMDP set a goal of three times ten to the eighth total nucleated cells per kilogram of recipient weight as a quality metric.
Volume-based collections are usually ten to fifteen millilitres per kilogram of recipient weight, and many centres cap the harvest at twenty millilitres per kilogram of donor weight.
During the harvest, the goal volume is refined by dividing the requested nucleated cell dose by the white cell count of the marrow collected so far.

Each pull matters. Some centres limit pulls to five millilitres to limit hemodilution; others take up to twenty with stylet replacement. Smaller pulls give higher cell concentrations, but the effect on final yield is not settled.

props.label: Goal volume = requested TNC ÷ marrow WBC

scenes.title: Same-day count, two-week potency
scenes.altText: Three assay cards. CD34 flow: standard of care for HPC enumeration; turnaround 40–60 min in one study (Tiwari 2023). CFU assay: cells plated in semisolid methylcellulose medium with growth factors; single progenitors grow into colonies counted by microscope (counted after 14 days in Gençer 2017); regarded as the gold-standard potency test because CFU number correlates with engraftment (Yusoff 2025); drawbacks: labour-intensive, poorly standardised, long turnaround. ALDH activity by flow cytometry: a newer method that correlated highly with CFU counts in cord blood, but published results on engraftment conflict.

cues.text: Counting and potency are different questions. Flow cytometric CD34 counting is the standard of care for counting progenitor cells, and in one study it took forty to sixty minutes: a same-day answer.

The colony-forming unit assay plates cells in a semisolid methylcellulose medium with growth factors. Each progenitor grows into a colony that is counted under the microscope. In one cord blood study, colonies were counted after fourteen days.
The colony assay is regarded as the gold standard for potency, because colony numbers correlate with engraftment. But it is labour-intensive, poorly standardised and slow.
A newer flow assay measures aldehyde dehydrogenase, or ALDH, activity. In cord blood it correlated highly with colony counts, but published results on engraftment are conflicting.

scenes.title: Engineered and pulsed cells
scenes.altText: CAR card (Fujiwara 2020; Ahmad 2020): a chimeric antigen receptor is an artificial transmembrane receptor joining an extracellular antigen-recognition domain (an antibody-derived scFv), a hinge domain, a transmembrane domain and an intracellular signalling domain in tandem; it redirects T-cell killing in an HLA-independent manner. Approval card (US FDA; Ahmad 2020 Table 1): tisagenlecleucel, anti-CD19, 30 August 2017 for B-cell precursor ALL in patients up to 25 years; axicabtagene ciloleucel, anti-CD19, 18 October 2017 for adult large B-cell lymphomas. Sipuleucel-T card (Graff 2015; Sutherland 2021): autologous cellular immunotherapy, FDA-approved 2010 for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer; antigen-presenting cells from leukapheresis are pulsed with PA2024 (PAP plus GM-CSF) and reinfused. Hook answers.

cues.text: A chimeric antigen receptor is an artificial receptor built from four parts in a row: an antigen-recognition domain taken from an antibody, a hinge, a transmembrane domain, and an internal signalling domain. It lets T cells recognise antigen without HLA.

In the United States, two anti-CD19 products were approved in 2017: tisagenlecleucel in August for B-cell precursor ALL in patients up to twenty-five, and axicabtagene ciloleucel in October for adult large B-cell lymphoma.

Sipuleucel-T is different: no engineered receptor. The patient’s own antigen-presenting cells are collected by leukapheresis, pulsed with a prostatic acid phosphatase and GM-CSF protein, and reinfused. It was approved in 2010 for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer.

Back to the hook. Small pulls, harvested to a nucleated cell dose per kilogram. CD34 flow for today, while the colony assay needs a long culture. And the young patient’s product is an anti-CD19 CAR T cell.

props.label: Small pulls · CD34 today · CD19 CAR

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “The CFU assay gives a quick potency result” (✓ colonies need a long culture, counted at 14 days in one study; CD34 flow is the same-day count); “Bigger pulls collect more marrow cells” (✓ smaller pulls give higher TNC concentrations and limit hemodilution); “CAR T cells need HLA to see their target” (✓ CAR recognition is HLA-independent).

cues.text: Trap one: the colony assay gives a quick potency answer. No: colonies need a long culture, fourteen days in one cord blood study. The same-day count is CD34 flow.
Trap two: bigger pulls collect more marrow cells. No: smaller pulls give higher nucleated cell concentrations and limit hemodilution.
Trap three: CAR T cells need HLA to see their target. No: the antibody-derived binding domain recognises antigen without HLA.

scenes.title: Dose, grow, steer
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “DOSE the marrow (nucleated cells per kilogram, small pulls), GROW the colonies (CFU needs a long culture), STEER the T cell (a CAR points it at CD19).” Tokens: dose = TNC/kg · grow = CFU · steer = CAR. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: dose, grow, steer. Dose the marrow by nucleated cells per kilogram, in small pulls. Grow the colonies, which needs a long culture. Steer the T cell, with a CAR pointed at CD19.

Where it breaks: the release-day count is CD34 flow, not colonies; dose goals and pull volumes differ between centres; approvals since 2017 have grown and are US rulings; and sipuleucel-T is steered by a pulsed antigen, not a CAR.

lines: Goals and pull sizes vary by centre
US approvals only; sipuleucel-T is no CAR

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Marrow: TNC per kg recipient · small pulls limit dilution”, “CD34 flow = today · CFU = long culture · CAR = no HLA needed”.

cues.text: Harvest marrow to a nucleated cell dose per kilogram with small pulls that limit blood dilution, use CD34 flow for a same-day count while the colony assay needs a long culture, and remember that a CAR lets T cells see antigen without HLA.

props.label: Marrow: TNC per kg recipient · small pulls limit dilution
CD34 flow = today · CFU = long culture · CAR = no HLA needed

explanation.what: Plain language: a marrow harvest is planned by how many cells the recipient needs per kilogram, and pulling small amounts at a time keeps the sample from being watered down with ordinary blood. Counting stem cells is fast, but proving they can grow needs a long culture (14 days in one study). CAR T cells are a patient’s T cells given a new, built receptor; sipuleucel-T is a patient’s own antigen-presenting cells loaded with a prostate protein. Scientific terms: total nucleated cell (TNC) dose, hemodilution, CD34 enumeration, colony-forming unit (CFU) assay, methylcellulose, aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH), chimeric antigen receptor (CAR), single-chain variable fragment (scFv), hinge, transmembrane and signalling domains, tisagenlecleucel, axicabtagene ciloleucel, sipuleucel-T, PA2024.
explanation.why: Harvesters limit the volume aspirated at one site to mitigate hemodilution, and data show higher nucleated cell concentrations with smaller pulls. Colony formation requires progenitors to proliferate and differentiate in culture, which is slow (colonies were counted at 14 days in one study), so a surface-marker count is used for same-day decisions. A CAR’s antibody-derived binding domain recognises surface antigen directly, so it does not depend on HLA presentation.
explanation.measure: NMDP goal: 3.0 × 10⁸ TNC/kg recipient weight; volume usually 10–15 mL/kg recipient, capped at 20 mL/kg donor by the NMDP and many centres; goal volume refined as requested TNC ÷ marrow WBC count. Pulls: 5 mL limit at some centres, up to 20 mL with stylet replacement at others. CD34 flow turnaround 40–60 min (one study); CFU colonies counted at 14 days (one study). CAR approvals (US): 30 August 2017 and 18 October 2017; sipuleucel-T 2010.
explanation.differs: Volume goal vs TNC dose goal; small vs large pulls; CD34 count (adequacy, same day) vs CFU (potency, long culture) vs ALDH (newer, faster, evidence still mixed); CAR T (engineered receptor, anti-CD19) vs sipuleucel-T (antigen-pulsed autologous APCs, prostate cancer).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the consequence of large-volume marrow pulls, the assay that gives a same-day adequacy answer, the parts of a CAR, or the 2017 anti-CD19 CAR T indications.

questions.stem: A transplant physician needs to know this afternoon whether a fresh apheresis HPC collection is adequate. Which test gives that same-day answer?

options.text: CD34+ cell enumeration by flow cytometry
options.rationale: Correct. Flow cytometric CD34 counting is the standard of care for HPC enumeration and took 40–60 minutes in one study.
Incorrect. It is the gold-standard potency test, but it needs a long culture (colonies were counted at 14 days in one study).
Incorrect. Sterility cultures check for contamination, not progenitor content.

options.text: ALDH activity assay as the routine release test
options.rationale: Incorrect. ALDH is a newer method whose engraftment data are still conflicting; CD34 flow is the standard of care.

questions.stem: During a marrow harvest, the operator switches from small pulls to large-volume pulls from the same site. What is the expected effect?

options.text: More hemodilution and a lower nucleated cell concentration
options.rationale: Correct. Harvesters limit pull volume to mitigate hemodilution, and smaller pulls give higher TNC concentrations.

options.text: A higher nucleated cell concentration in each pull
options.rationale: Incorrect. The data point the other way: smaller pulls give higher TNC concentrations.

options.text: A higher CD34+ cell concentration in each pull
options.rationale: Incorrect. Pull volume is limited to mitigate hemodilution; it is smaller pulls that give higher cell concentrations.

options.text: No change, because only total volume matters
options.rationale: Incorrect. Harvest goals are set as nucleated cells per kilogram, so the concentration of each pull matters.

questions.stem: Which statement about chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells is correct?

options.text: The receptor joins an antibody-derived binding domain, a hinge, a transmembrane domain and a signalling domain, and recognises antigen without HLA
options.rationale: Correct. These four domains in tandem redirect T-cell killing in an HLA-independent manner.

options.text: CAR T cells recognise their target only when it is presented on donor-matched HLA
Sipuleucel-T was the first CAR T product approved in the United States
options.rationale: Incorrect. Sipuleucel-T is antigen-pulsed autologous antigen-presenting cells for prostate cancer, not an engineered T-cell receptor.

options.text: The two US CAR T products approved in 2017 targeted CD20 on myeloma cells
options.rationale: Incorrect. Both 2017 products targeted CD19, for B-cell precursor ALL and large B-cell lymphoma.

accuracyFlags.issue: Hit 8 gives 2–3 × 10⁸ viable nucleated cells/kg (~700 mL for a 70-kg adult). The NMDP Marrow Alliance white paper gives a goal TNC dose of 3.0 × 10⁸/kg recipient weight as a quality metric and usual volumes of 10–15 mL/kg recipient; no 2 × 10⁸ minimum was found (~700 mL for 70 kg is consistent with the low end of 10–15 mL/kg recipient). The lesson teaches the source goal.

Hit 8 gives 3–5 mL per pull. The NMDP white paper reports that some centres limit pulls to 5 mL while others take up to 20 mL with stylet replacement; smaller pulls give higher TNC concentrations, but effects on final yield and outcomes are undetermined. Technique-dependent.

Hit 13’s 2017 CAR T approvals are US FDA rulings; Philippine registration is not covered. The October 2017 axicabtagene ciloleucel approval was for adult large B-cell lymphomas (DLBCL among them), and the August 2017 tisagenlecleucel approval was for B-cell precursor ALL in patients up to 25 years.
